title: POC Weekly - Latency Tuning - Novapay

Agreed next steps: run focused microbenchmarks, try kernel A/B, tweak streaming chunk size, and share tuned config and results by Friday.

transcript:
[00:00] Sam Patel (AE): All right thanks everyone for hopping on. we did last week's run, um we're going to go over the TTFT numbers and next tuning steps. Jordan, you want to kick us off with the quick summary?
[00:12] Jordan Lee (SE): Yeah sure. so quick recap — we ingested the 5k request trace you sent, ran it against the redwood-hosted POC endpoint with streaming enabled and disabled. baseline TTFT with streaming off was around 180 to 210 ms median depending on payload, with p95 around 420. with streaming enabled and chunk size 64 tokens, median dropped to ~150ms, p95 to ~360ms. payloads with long prefix (2.5k tokens) pushed TTFT up, as expected.
[00:45] Maya Chen (CTO): Quick clarification — when you say TTFT are you including network egress, or is that server-side only?
[00:51] Jordan Lee (SE): Good call — the numbers I quoted are server-side measured in the runtime, so excludes client-side network. Alex, we can add your observed client RTT to map to end-to-end.
[01:02] Alex Rivera (SRE): Yeah on our side average network adds about 20 to 30 ms inside our VPC region. so end-to-end with streaming we were seeing around 180ms median for typical 512 token requests.
[01:15] Priya Kumar (ML Engineer): For our traffic mix, 70% of requests are under 512 tokens, 20% 512-2k, and about 10% >2k. so the long tail is small but important for latency SLOs.
[01:28] Sam Patel (AE): Perfect. so target we discussed was sub-120ms TTFT median for the core 70% — is that still the right bar?
[01:35] Maya Chen (CTO): yes that's what the payments UX team wants, under 120ms on median end-to-end. p95 SLA is less strict but we want it as low as possible.
[01:44] Jordan Lee (SE): Ok tactically we have a couple levers: streaming (reduce TTFT by emitting partial tokens earlier), smaller initial decode chunk, kernel selection for short-seq optimizations, kv cache warmup, and quantization profiles. each has tradeoffs.
[01:57] Jordan Lee (SE): On kernels — we tested kernel_v2 which has optimized attention for short sequences and it shaved about 20-30ms off median for <512 requests, with negligible quality impact. switching kernels is a runtime flag, but on some GPU types we saw slightly higher variance.
[02:14] Priya Kumar (ML Engineer): Did you quantify variance? our concern is p95 getting worse even if median improves.
[02:20] Jordan Lee (SE): yes, good question. for kernel_v2 median improved, p95 improved slightly for short seqs, but for mixed workloads with many long sequences we saw p95 bump by ~30ms due to slower fallback path. needs A/B on your traffic mix.
[02:35] Maya Chen (CTO): What about TTFT improvements from early token streaming vs partial logits? we tried enabling streaming in our dev test but saw a small quality shift — hallucination-like cutoffs.
[02:47] Jordan Lee (SE): Streaming just changes delivery, not model decode. hallucination/quality changes usually come from shorter decode windows or chunked prompt processing. we recommended keeping the same decode strategy and just stream tokens as they are produced. also pruning first-token softmax can reduce latency but not recommended without evals.
[03:05] Alex Rivera (SRE): On infra, we can pin instances to dedicated pools. the dedicated run reduced jitter by about 10-15ms on our tests. cost tradeoff though.
[03:15] Sam Patel (AE): Right. reminder that Redwood Dedicated gives reserved capacity and lower variance, but costs more. For the POC we can simulate dedicated capacity on a burstable node pool to reproduce behavior. Jordan, can you explain the KV cache warmup note?
[03:29] Jordan Lee (SE): Sure — for conversational flows with shared prompts we can warm KV cache by priming with common prefixes or using a prefix cache at the serving layer. that reduces recompute for repeated contexts and lowers TTFT for subsequent calls by ~10-20ms in our experiments. downside: memory usage and cache eviction complexity.
[03:45] Priya Kumar (ML Engineer): We do have high reuse for the payment prompt templates so warmup seems promising. what's the recommended cache TTL?
[03:52] Jordan Lee (SE): start with short TTL — 30 to 60 seconds — and measure. TTL depends on your concurrency. Jordan: (laugh) sorry cause name collision, but yes 30s is a good starting point.
[04:03] Maya Chen (CTO): On quantization, we tested 4-bit QKV on smaller model variant. we saw a small drop in perplexity but inference latency improved slightly for larger sequences. did Redwood test 4-bit on your kernels?
[04:15] Jordan Lee (SE): We did. 4-bit quantization with the updated kernels gives a compounding latency win for long sequences, but for short sequences the overhead of dequantization can offset gains. recommendation: use hybrid profiles — 8-bit for short-seq hot path, 4-bit for long-seq batch processing.
[04:32] Alex Rivera (SRE): That hybrid approach sounds complex to route. can Redwood runtime auto-route by sequence length?
[04:38] Jordan Lee (SE): Yes, we can set routing rules based on sequence length. policy engine can pick model/quant/profile per-request. we can demo a rule set.
[04:46] Sam Patel (AE): Ok let's get concrete — Jordan, what are the two configs you want Novapay to run this week?
[04:52] Jordan Lee (SE): Run A: streaming enabled, kernel_v2, hybrid quant with short-seq 8-bit, long-seq 4-bit, prefix KV cache TTL 30s. Run B: streaming disabled, kernel_v1 (current), 8-bit quant global, no KV cache. We'll compare median TTFT and p95 CPU/GPU stalls.
[05:09] Priya Kumar (ML Engineer): Sounds good. what's the microbenchmark script look like — synthetic or replay?
[05:14] Jordan Lee (SE): We'll provide a replay harness that uses your 1k sample trace with original timing removed (we push requests as fast as single-client concurrency you choose) plus a synthetic burst profile. Script will output TTFT median/p95, token throughput, GPU utilization, and trace of kernel times.
[05:28] Alex Rivera (SRE): On instrumentation — we need the runtime traces in the same format as our perf tooling. can you include JSON lines logs and a CSV of per-request metrics?
[05:36] Jordan Lee (SE): yes we'll include both. also include GPU counters (SM utilization, mem BW) where the environment supports NVIDIA metrics.
[05:45] Maya Chen (CTO): timeline — can you deliver configs and scripts by Thursday so we run Friday?
[05:50] Sam Patel (AE): we can deliver by Thursday EOD. Jordan do you confirm?
[05:53] Jordan Lee (SE): Confirm. I'll attach instructions on kernel toggles — note for some older CUDA stacks kernel_v2 needs a minor driver bump; we'll flag that.
[06:02] Priya Kumar (ML Engineer): about p99 — we care less but would like to know tail causes. can you surface whether tails are queuing, mem thrash, or decoder stalls?
[06:10] Jordan Lee (SE): Yep the microbenchmarks will include breakdown: scheduling queuing, kernel execution, mem copies, and decoder time. we'll try to attribute p95/p99 to top causes.
[06:19] Alex Rivera (SRE): Also curious on cold-start TTFT. We saw first request after idle spikes a lot.
[06:25] Jordan Lee (SE): That's usually model load time or JIT warmup. For low-latency use we recommend one of: keep-warm pods, smaller boot bundles, or use the dedicated runtime with pre-warmed model. we can simulate a keep-warm at 1 qps.
[06:38] Maya Chen (CTO): Any security blockers for switching kernels or enabling streaming?
[06:43] Sam Patel (AE): No, kernel choice is an internal runtime optimization and doesn't change model outputs or data routing. streaming is just delivery. both are fine from a compliance perspective. we'll share the security note in the docs.
[06:52] Priya Kumar (ML Engineer): Great. can Jordan also include recommended inference paths for our latency budget? like a simple decision table?
[06:58] Jordan Lee (SE): Yep, we'll include a short decision table: if seq_len < 600 -> kernel_v2 + streaming + 8-bit; if seq_len 600-2k -> kernel_v1 + hybrid quant, if >2k -> batch long-seq path with 4-bit. We'll include config snippets.
[07:15] Sam Patel (AE): ok let's summarize next steps and owners. Sam to share config + security note by 2026-06-11. Jordan to send harness and kernel docs by same date. Novapay (Priya/Alex) to run microbench and return results by 2026-06-12. schedule infra deep dive w/Novapay week of 2026-06-15.
[07:35] Maya Chen (CTO): That works. one more ask — can Redwood run an A/B with our production traffic mirror if we give a temporary read-only mirror?
[07:44] Jordan Lee (SE): We can plan for a mirror test; need legal/ops signoff. Sam will coordinate.
[07:50] Alex Rivera (SRE): I'll surface what we need on our side — perf counters, histogram of sequence lengths and current concurrency.
[07:57] Sam Patel (AE): Great. thanks everyone. we'll follow up in email with the artifacts.
[08:01] Maya Chen (CTO): thanks all.
[08:02] (call ends)
